We learned yesterday that a judge allowed a $32 billion lawsuit to proceed alleging that Apple Photos' facial recognition feature violates state privacy laws.

While the two companies sit at opposite ends of the privacy spectrum, observers have conflated this case with Meta's use of facial recognition. The judge's decision to allow the case to proceed means the court fundamentally misunderstands how that feature works...

The Earlier Lawsuit Against Meta

To properly understand the situation, we first need to go back to a facial recognition lawsuit against Meta dating back to 2015.

Because that facial recognition was performed on Meta's servers, and Meta was able to identify who those people were, the company did indeed break the law, and was eventually forced to settle for $650 million.

Apple is now being sued under that same Illinois law — the Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) — which prohibits companies from collecting biometric data without consent.

Apple's Approach Is Fundamentally Different

There's a huge problem with the lawsuit's claim: Apple absolutely does not collect any biometric data to power facial recognition in the Apple Photos app. As Apple noted in a machine learning research paper published in 2021, the recognition algorithm runs entirely on-device.

Beyond that, all the iPhone is doing is telling you "these photos all feature the same person" — it has absolutely no idea who that person is. The only person who can put a name to those photos is the iPhone's user.

Apple says as much in its privacy policy related to photos.

This lawsuit is in its sixth year in the court system, but a few minutes of research reveals that the lawsuit's claims are simply wrong. To me, this is genuinely unbelievable.

Courts and legislatures should be actively affirming Apple's privacy-preserving approach rather than conflating it with the privacy-destroying approach of companies like Meta.

This is just another example of courts and legislatures fundamentally misunderstanding the technology they're trying to regulate. The most obvious example, of course, is end-to-end encryption — multiple countries have threatened or even attempted to ban end-to-end encryption, without any understanding of how it actually works.

Of course, I understand that judges and politicians can't be experts in every area they need to deal with. But they do have access to experts, and to me, it's baffling that a lawsuit and the related legislation can continue to make its way through the system for years without anyone pointing out these fundamental errors.
